catalog_quote: Most technical expressions remain unchanged in English as in Tables 5(b) and are mostly maintained with the stress of the English Language without the tones of Agwagune being imposed on them. These include words such as menu, delete, laptop, software. Other words maintained in English include mathematical expressions and the language of science. They are employed in a code-mix when used in speech. [Ugot 2013: 268] ... The languages we are considering are both tone languages of West Africa. [Huffman 1987: 68] ... data from one speaker of Agwagwune, a little-studied language of Nigeria which has no oral/nasal contrast in vowels. [Huffman 1987: 70]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., text, extracted text) and located the passage on PDF page 8 = printed p. 268 (footer 'Copyright IAARR 2013.. 268'), immediately after Table 5 'Borrowings from English': 'Most technical expressions remain unchanged in English as in Tables 5(b) and are mostly maintained with the stress of the English Language without the tones of Agwagune being imposed on them. These include words such as menu, delete, laptop, software.' Verbatim match. a full-text search for stress/accent the full text confirms this is the only occurrence of 'stress' in the article; 'tone' occurs only here too, but all Agwagune data in Tables 1-5 carry H/L tone diacritics. The corroborating Huffman 1987 line…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word-stress placement is stated by any source opened. Agwagune is described as a tone language (Huffman 1987; Ugot's data are marked with high/low tones and tonal alternations are described); Ugot 2013 contrasts native Agwagune tones with English stress, which is retained only on unassimilated English technical loans. Nothing says whether native words have a stress prominence at all.
new_statements.exceptions: Only that unassimilated English technical loans (menu, delete, laptop, software) keep English stress rather than receiving Agwagune tones (Ugot 2013: 268).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Ugot 2013 discusses isolated lexical items (loanwords); Huffman 1987 is an instrumental nasalization study of one Agwagwune speaker reading words in a frame sentence. Neither is a phonological description; the tone-language label is incidental in both.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the prestige variety Agwagune/Agwagwune proper (Egip-Ipa clan, Biase LGA) = Glottolog agwa1247 'Nuclear Agwagwune'; Huffman 1987 records one speaker of 'Agwagwune'. The inaccessible Williams 2011 phonology describes the Adim dialect (Glottolog dialect under agwa1247; Ethnologue lists Adim as a dialect of Gwune), not the prestige variety.

tone_statements.citation: Ukam, Edadi Ilem. 2017. Acoustic manifestation of English lexical stress pattern by native Erei speakers. English Linguistics Research 6(4): 38-50. Sciedu Press. DOI 10.5430/elr.v6n4p38.
tone_statements.quote: 2.4 Tonal Nature of Erei. Two tones are used in Erei, namely high (´) and low (ᶥ) which help listeners to differentiate words (Inya, 2011). Just as stress is phonemic in English (such as, ex-port switching from noun to verb, if the stress shifts from the first syllable of a disyllabic word to the second), tone is also phonemic in Erei. A word may have two distinct meanings by simply changing the tones (Ukam, 2015). Erei-English bilingual speakers transfer these tones in their process of speaking English. The primary stress is equated to a high tone, whereas all others become low tone with no secondary stress (Ukam, 2015).
tone_statements.locator: p. 42, section 2.4 'Tonal Nature of Erei'; cf. abstract p. 38: 'The feature [lexical stress] is not observable in Erei, which is a tonal language, where all the syllables or vowels in a word are given strong form.'

sources.quote: 2.4 Tonal Nature of Erei. Two tones are used in Erei, namely high (´) and low (ᶥ) which help listeners to differentiate words (Inya, 2011). sources.locator: p. 42, section 2.4 'Tonal Nature of Erei'; cf. abstract p. 38: 'The feature [lexical stress] is not observable in Erei, which is a tonal language, where all the syllables or vowels in a word are given strong form.'
sources.note: Erei is a tonal language with two tones, high and low; tone is phonemic (minimal pairs by tone alone); Erei-English bilinguals map English primary stress to H and all other syllables to L. Also states English-type lexical stress 'is not observable in Erei' and that Erei is 'not stress-timed' / 'syllable-timed' (pp. 38, 46-47). No mention of downstep, contour tones or grammatical tone.
